style: steady, curious history narrator, quietly adventurous

lines.text: For centuries the oceans kept the continents apart. Then sailors set out into the unknown, and in a few hundred years the whole world was joined.
Long before Columbus, around the year 1000, the Norseman Leif Erikson reached North America and called it Vinland. A Norse site in Newfoundland proves the sagas right.
Two centuries later, the Venetian merchant Marco Polo crossed Asia to the court of Kublai Khan, and his book opened European eyes to the riches of the East.
Then came Ibn Battuta of Morocco, who spent some thirty years on the road, from West Africa to China, and wrote it all down.
In Ming China, the admiral Zheng He was born, a man who would lead some of the largest fleets the world had ever seen.
In Portugal, Prince Henry, later called the Navigator, backed voyage after voyage down the coast of West Africa, though he hardly sailed himself.
From 1405, Zheng He's treasure fleets crossed the Indian Ocean seven times, as far as East Africa, showing off Ming power. Then China turned inward.
Portugal, meanwhile, took Ceuta in North Africa in 1415, the first step of an empire of trading posts that would reach from Brazil to Macau.
In 1488 Bartolomeu Dias rounded the southern tip of Africa, the Cape of Good Hope, and proved there was a sea route to Asia.
John Cabot, an Italian sailing for England, would reach the coast of North America in 1497.
Christopher Columbus, born in Genoa, would sail west for Spain and reach the Caribbean, though to the end he believed he had found Asia.
Afonso de Albuquerque would seize Goa, Malacca and Hormuz, and build Portugal a chain of forts across Asia.
Amerigo Vespucci, sailing along South America, saw that it was a new continent, not Asia. The Americas would carry his name.
Across the ocean, Moctezuma the Second would rule the Aztec Empire, until he met the Spaniards in his own capital.
Pedro Alvares Cabral, bound for India, would swing far west and reach Brazil in 1500, claiming it for Portugal.
Vasco da Gama would make the first voyage by sea from Europe to India, a route that made Portugal rich.
Vasco Nunez de Balboa would cross Panama in 1513 and become the first European to see the Pacific from the Americas.
Francisco Pizarro would lead a small band into the Inca Empire, capture its ruler and take Peru for Spain.
Ferdinand Magellan, a Portuguese sailing for Spain, would find the strait at the bottom of South America that bears his name.
Hernan Cortes would land in Mexico in 1519 and, with Indigenous allies, bring down the Aztec Empire.
And Juan Sebastian Elcano, a Basque sailor, would bring Magellan's last ship home, the first to sail all the way around the world.
Jacques Cartier would sail up the St Lawrence for France, and give us a local word for a village, kanata, the source of the name Canada.
Then, in 1492, Columbus set sail with three ships and crossed the Atlantic to the Caribbean. He would make four voyages in all.
What followed was the Columbian exchange. Potatoes, maize and horses crossed the ocean, and so did smallpox, which killed vast numbers in the Americas.
From those voyages grew the Spanish Empire, whose silver mines would shape world trade and make Spanish a global language.
In 1494 Spain and Portugal drew a line down the Atlantic and split the new lands between them. It is why Brazil speaks Portuguese today.
In 1497 Vasco da Gama sailed round Africa and across the Indian Ocean to Calicut, opening a direct sea road between Europe and Asia.
The darkest trade followed: for more than three centuries, millions of Africans were shipped in chains across the Atlantic to work the plantations and mines.
In the Andes, Atahualpa would win a civil war to rule the Incas, only to be captured and executed by Pizarro's men.
In 1507 a map by Martin Waldseemuller was the first to show a separate new continent, and to call it America.
Francisco de Orellana would become the first European to travel the whole length of the Amazon, in 1542.
Gerardus Mercator, a Flemish mapmaker, would draw a map in 1569 that let sailors steer by straight lines, a projection still in use.
In 1519 five Spanish ships set out to reach the Spice Islands by sailing west. Magellan died on the way, but three years later one ship came home.
Meanwhile in Mexico, Cortes and his allies besieged and took the Aztec capital, where Mexico City stands today.
A decade later, Pizarro's small force, helped by disease and an Inca civil war, began the conquest of the Inca Empire.
England joined the race. Francis Drake raided Spanish treasure ships and, from 1577 to 1580, sailed all the way around the world.
Henry Hudson would search for a northern way to Asia, and leave his name on a river, a strait and a bay before his crew set him adrift.
From 1565 Spanish galleons sailed between Manila and Mexico, linking Asia and the Americas for two and a half centuries.
The Dutchman Willem Janszoon would, in 1606, become the first European known to land in Australia.
Samuel de Champlain would found Quebec in 1608 and explore the Great Lakes, earning the title father of New France.
In 1600 Elizabeth the First chartered the English East India Company. A trading firm, it would grow into the ruler of much of India.
Two years later the Dutch founded their own, selling shares to the public. With fleets and forts across Asia, it led the spice trade.
Abel Tasman would sail from Batavia in 1642 and become the first European known to reach Tasmania and New Zealand.
In 1607 English settlers founded Jamestown in Virginia, the first English colony in America that lasted.
In 1620 the Mayflower carried the Pilgrims across the Atlantic to found Plymouth Colony, a voyage that became an American founding story.
The Dutch built a trading town on Manhattan, New Amsterdam. In 1664 the English took it, and named it New York.
Vitus Bering, a Dane in Russian service, would find the narrow strait between Asia and America that now bears his name.
John Harrison, a clockmaker, would build timekeepers accurate enough at sea to solve the riddle of longitude, so ships could finally know where they were.
And James Cook would make three great voyages across the Pacific, before being killed in a clash at Hawaii.
His ship was the Endeavour, a converted coal ship, which carried him to Tahiti, New Zealand and the east coast of Australia.
In 1768 Cook sailed to Tahiti to watch Venus cross the Sun, then charted New Zealand and eastern Australia, as his scientists gathered plants and animals new to Europe.
By Cook's time, the oceans no longer divided the world. They joined it, for better and for worse.
